title: A logic capturing logarithmic space
area: Database theory and finite model theory
formal: Does there exist one effective logic \(\mathcal L\), in the precise sense below, whose sentences define exactly all deterministic logarithmic-space Boolean properties of finite unordered relational structures, for every finite relational vocabulary?
why: This asks whether all order-independent queries evaluable with logarithmic working memory have an effective logical language with exactly that expressive power. It would connect a central low-space computation model to a complete account of queries on finite relational data, beyond the familiar setting where an input order is supplied.
status_note: The general objective and the failure of CLogspace were checked in the 2019 full text. The standard effective capturing convention was checked in the 2015 author survey. The June 2026 FC-Datalog abstract and history were checked for domain and date; its full proofs were not independently reviewed. Bounded later searches through 14 September 2026 located no matching general existence or impossibility result. This is not an exhaustive certification of current openness.

progress.text: CLogspace is introduced and proved to be a strict fragment of logarithmic space; the broader search for a capturing logic remains in the discussion.
The revised FC-Datalog manuscript states LOGSPACE-capturing results for fragments on strings. Its domain restriction prevents these results from settling the present target.

importance.reason: A broad descriptive-complexity existence question for a central resource class, with consequences for the expressive limits of order-independent database queries. It is distinct from improving one proposed recursion operator.

sentences: The input is a finite relational structure with no distinguished ordering of its elements.
The question asks for an effective logic expressing exactly all isomorphism-invariant Boolean queries decidable in deterministic logarithmic space.
Each sentence must compile to a halting evaluation algorithm with a certified logarithmic workspace bound.
The proposed CLogspace logic is known to miss some such queries, while ordered structures and strings admit stronger capturing results.
A solution would settle a broad descriptive-complexity question linking small-memory computation to the expressive power of logical queries.

definitions:
A vocabulary \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A \(\tau\)-structure \(A\) has a finite nonempty domain and, for each \(r\)-ary symbol, an \(r\)-ary relation on that domain. An isomorphism is a bijection preserving and reflecting every relation. A Boolean property of \(\tau\)-structures is a class closed under isomorphism. The mathematical input supplies no distinguished ordering of its elements.

For computation, label the domain by \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\). Encode \(n\) in unary followed by all relation truth tables in the vocabulary order and lexicographic tuple order, using one bit per tuple. Write \(N\) for the full encoding length. All labelings of a structure are valid encodings. A property is in deterministic logarithmic space, denoted \(\mathrm L\), if a fixed deterministic Turing machine halts and decides it correctly on every such encoding using at most \(C\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) work-tape cells for some fixed positive integer \(C\). Machines have a read-only two-way input tape, a finite control, and a fixed finite number of work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. Work space counts all cells visited on the work tapes; the input tape is not writable. They have no oracle, advice, auxiliary input, or random bits. A machine may use the encoding order internally, but its answer must be the same on all isomorphic inputs.

The proposed logic has a decidable set of finite binary encodings of pairs \((\tau,\varphi)\), where \(\varphi\) is a sentence over \(\tau\). Each valid sentence has a Boolean satisfaction relation \(A\models\varphi\) on all finite nonempty \(\tau\)-structures, invariant under isomorphism. There must be one total computable compiler that, on a valid pair, outputs a deterministic Turing machine \(M_\varphi\) and a positive integer \(C_\varphi\). For every valid encoding of every \(\tau\)-structure, \(M_\varphi\) must halt, return its satisfaction value, and use at most \(C_\varphi\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) work cells. On invalid sentence encodings the compiler may return a fixed error symbol. Syntax checking and compilation are not required to run in logarithmic space or polynomial time.

Expressive completeness requires that for every finite \(\tau\) and every isomorphism-invariant \(\mathrm L\) property \(Q\) of its structures, there is one fixed \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\) such that \[ \forall A:\quad A\models\varphi\iff A\in Q.\] The sentence and its space constant may depend on \(Q\) and \(\tau\), but not on \(A\). The same syntax and compiler work across all vocabularies. No computable translation from arbitrary invariant machines to sentences is required. There is no uniform logarithmic-space requirement when the sentence is part of the evaluation input. A relational query with a fixed tuple of distinguished elements can be represented as a Boolean property in a vocabulary expanded by singleton unary relations marking those elements; the target uses the Boolean convention throughout.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a logic exists, including decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective evaluation with certified per-sentence space constants, and expressive completeness; or prove that no logic meets all those conditions. The formalism and its semantics must be specified, rather than merely assigning an uninterpreted name to each logarithmic-space property. A result for one candidate logic or for a restricted family of input structures does not settle this general existence question.

context_blocks.text: The source motivation is computation on large relational inputs with very little working memory. A representation necessarily labels the elements, but a query about the abstract structure must not change when those labels are permuted. Capturing asks for both expressive completeness and an effective resource-bounded evaluation of every sentence.

The 2019 paper constructs CLogspace as a logic for computations that preserve input symmetries. Its objects are finite sets built from input elements and further finite sets, equipped with size annotations and restricted recursion. Theorem 27 proves that this particular logic is strictly weaker than logarithmic space. That negative result concerns a candidate, not the existence of any capturing logic.

The saved passage asks whether ideas from CLogspace can yield a stronger logic. It specifies no formal class of permitted extensions. This card makes explicit the general logic-existence objective discussed in the same paper’s introduction and Section 5; it does not require a particular extension grammar or claim that CLogspace itself captures the class. The effective-syntax and compiler requirements follow the standard capturing convention, with the space bound stated separately here.

An externally supplied order changes the descriptive problem. The 2019 source recalls that deterministic transitive-closure logic captures logarithmic space on ordered structures. More recently, Bell, Day and Freydenberger obtain LOGSPACE-capturing fragments for string queries; the June 2026 abstract concerns strings, not arbitrary unordered relational inputs.
